### Network Position as an Instrument {#sec-network-peer-iv}

Peer effects are among the hardest things in applied work to identify, and the reason is an
identification failure rather than a data problem. @manski1993identification named it the
reflection problem: if everyone in a group is influenced by the group mean, and the group mean is
the average of the people being influenced, the endogenous effect (my outcome responds to my
peers' outcomes) cannot be separated from the contextual effect (my outcome responds to my peers'
characteristics) or from correlated effects (we share an environment).

@bramoulle2009identification showed that the failure is specific to the group structure rather
than intrinsic. When peer groups overlap only partially, network position supplies instruments.

#### The Linear-in-Means Model on a Network

Let $G$ be a row-normalized adjacency matrix, so $Gy$ is the average outcome among a unit's
links. The model is

$$
y = \beta_{\text{endo}} \, G y + \beta_{\text{own}} \, x + \beta_{\text{cxt}} \, G x + \varepsilon .
$$

The regressor $Gy$ is endogenous by construction: it contains $\varepsilon$ for every neighbour,
and the system is simultaneous. Under the classic setup where everyone in a group is linked to
everyone else, $G$ is the same for all members and $Gx$ is collinear with what identification
would require, which is the reflection problem in matrix form.

When the network is intransitive, meaning that some of your friends' friends are not your friends,
the characteristics of those second-degree contacts are the instrument. They affect your outcome
only through your friends' outcomes, which is exactly the exclusion restriction, and they are not
collinear with $x$ or $Gx$ because the network is not complete. The instruments are $G^2 x$, and
sometimes $G^3 x$.

@degiorgi2010identification exploit the same structure using partially overlapping peer groups
generated by university course assignment.

#### Demonstration

```{r netiv-demo, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(igraph)
library(ivreg)
set.seed(505)

peer <- function(n = 600, b_endo = 0.4, b_cxt = 0.3, b_own = 1) {
  g <- sample_gnp(n, 4 / n)                  # sparse, so largely intransitive
  A <- as.matrix(as_adjacency_matrix(g))
  G <- A / pmax(rowSums(A), 1)               # row-normalized peer matrix

  x   <- rnorm(n)
  eps <- rnorm(n)
  # Solve the simultaneous system for the reduced form.
  y <- as.vector(solve(diag(n) - b_endo * G) %*%
                   (b_own * x + b_cxt * (G %*% x) + eps))

  Gy <- as.vector(G %*% y); Gx <- as.vector(G %*% x)
  G2x <- as.vector(G %*% Gx); G3x <- as.vector(G %*% G2x)

  c(OLS = unname(coef(lm(y ~ Gy + x + Gx))["Gy"]),
    IV  = unname(coef(ivreg(y ~ Gy + x + Gx | x + Gx + G2x + G3x))["Gy"]))
}

round(rowMeans(replicate(150, peer())), 3)
```

Least squares overstates the endogenous peer effect, roughly 0.63 against a true 0.40, because
$Gy$ carries the neighbours' errors. Instrumenting with the characteristics of second- and
third-degree contacts recovers the truth.

#### Why This Is Harder Than It Looks

The simulation succeeds because the network is exogenous, correctly measured, and generated
without homophily. Each of those is a strong assumption, and @angrist2014perils argues that the
whole enterprise is more fragile than its econometric packaging suggests.

Network formation is the first problem. People choose their friends, and they choose them partly
on the unobservables that drive the outcome. If links form on latent similarity, then $G^2 x$ is
correlated with $\varepsilon$ through the same latent trait, and the instrument is invalid for
precisely the reason the design was meant to solve. Fixed effects at the network or group level
absorb some of this but not selection into links within a group.

Measurement is the second. Survey instruments that cap the number of friends a respondent may
name truncate the network, and the resulting $G$ is wrong in a way that is correlated with
popularity. Because the instruments are powers of $G$, measurement error compounds.

The third is mechanical, and it is the point @angrist2014perils presses hardest. Regressing an
outcome on a leave-out group mean of the same variable produces a nonzero coefficient even when
no social interaction exists at all, because the group mean and the individual outcome share
sampling variation. Much of the peer-effects literature is, on this reading, a weak-instrument
problem in which the 2SLS estimate is pulled toward a mechanical artifact. The remedy is to check
what the estimator returns under a null of no peer effect in the actual network and group sizes at
hand, rather than trusting asymptotics.

The estimand deserves the same care. $\beta_{\text{endo}}$ is a local effect on the margin defined
by the network, and the social multiplier implied by extrapolating it, $1/(1 - \beta_{\text{endo}})$,
is a long-run equilibrium object that the design does not identify.

#### Practice

1.  Report the intransitivity of the network. If the clustering coefficient is near one the
    instruments are close to collinear and the design has little content.
2.  Report first-stage strength for $G^2 x$ specifically. These instruments are often weak, and
    weak-instrument-robust inference should be the default rather than an afterthought.
3.  Simulate the null. Generate outcomes with no peer effect on the observed network and group
    sizes, and show the estimator returns zero.
4.  Address network formation directly. Include group fixed effects, and where the network was
    assigned rather than chosen, say so, because that is the strongest version of the design.
5.  Report how the network was measured and whether the survey capped nominations.
6.  Do not report a social multiplier as though it were estimated.
